title: Into the postdoctoral wormhole
text: My PhD thesis is finally under review. After five years of trawl surveys, stomach contents, null models and more R scripts than I’d like to admit, I’m stepping into what I like to call the postdoctoral wormhole: that strange space between finishing a thesis and figuring out what comes next.

title: Into the postdoctoral wormhole
text:
Where I’m coming from
My thesis looked at the fish and invertebrate assemblages of San Antonio Bay, in northern Patagonia: which species and traits make it through the filters of a highly variable bay, who eats whom, and how all of this connects with the local artisanal fishery.
Along the way, I discovered a second passion: how we do science. Messy folders, undocumented data, analyses nobody (including me, six months later) could reproduce. That led me to train as an open science instructor at the LMU Open Science Center, to join SORTEE, to become an Ocean Data Steward, and to spend a summer thinking about study design and reporting at the Meta-Science Summer School in Berlin.

title: Into the postdoctoral wormhole
text:
Where I’m going
I want to bring those two worlds together: metascience in marine ecology. How are ecological data collected, reported and shared? How can we make them easier to trust and reuse? I’m currently looking for postdoctoral opportunities in this space.

title: Maité A. Barrena
text:
Hi, I’m Mai 🌊

I’m a marine ecologist (she/her) finishing my PhD at the National University of Comahue and a CONICET doctoral fellow at the Faculty of Marine Sciences and CIMAS in San Antonio Oeste, northern Patagonia.

I study how coastal fish and invertebrate assemblages of San Antonio Bay are assembled and how they change through time: which species and traits pass the environmental filters of a highly variable bay, how they are connected in food webs, and how all of this relates to the local artisanal fishery.
I also care deeply about how we do science. I trained as an open science instructor at the LMU Open Science Center, I’m an Ocean Data Steward, and I’m moving toward metascience in marine ecology: studying how ecological data are collected, reported and shared, so they can be trusted and reused.

title: Open Science & Research Data
text:
Ecology relies more and more on long-term monitoring, satellite products and large shared datasets. Whether those data can be trusted and reused depends on how we organise, document and report our work.

I want to help close that gap in marine ecology in two ways: by teaching practical, reproducible workflows to fellow researchers, and by studying research practices themselves (metascience). I’m especially interested in data editing and data stewardship for ecological journals and observatories.

title: Research
text:
Study area: San Antonio Bay and the San Matías Gulf, northern Patagonia



San Antonio Bay is a hypersaline, macrotidal coastal bay on the San Matías Gulf (Río Negro, Argentina). Tides empty and refill its channels twice a day, temperature swings strongly between seasons, and an artisanal fishery has worked its waters for decades.
That variability makes it a natural laboratory to ask how coastal communities are assembled, how stable they are, and how people and ecosystems are linked.

title: Research
text:
Research lines

  
  
    In reviewPhD · chapter 1
    Persistent functional structure in a variable bay
    Species come and go with the seasons, yet the functional structure of the fish assemblage persists. Using null models, β-diversity and functional trajectories, we show it emerges from hierarchical environmental filtering and ontogenetic turnover.
    Barrena et al. · Ecology and Evolution (in review)
  



  
  
    In preparationPhD · chapter 3
    Who eats whom: trophic ecology of coastal fishes
    Diet analyses of the dominant coastal fishes, grouped into predator guilds and prey functional groups, reveal how the food web is organised and how opportunistic predators respond to new prey such as the invasive green crab.
  



  
  
    PublishedPhD · chapter 4
    The fish assemblage and the artisanal fishery through time
    Comparing current surveys with historical records to understand how the coastal fish assemblage and the catch of San Antonio Bay's artisanal fishers have changed, and how fishers perceive those changes.
    Barrena et al. 2025 · Marine and Fishery Sciences · doi
  



  
  
    In preparationCollaboration · data & code
    A hypersaline bay–gulf front
    Hydrography and chlorophyll-a patterns across the San Antonio Bay – San Matías Gulf frontal system. My role: data curation, analysis workflow and a reproducible repository.
    Saad et al. · GitHub repository
  



  
  
    Hackweek projectFish-PACE HackWeek 2026
    A glimpse of food webs from space
    Linking satellite-derived phytoplankton functional types (NASA PACE) with fish functional traits from NOAA bottom trawl surveys on the Northeast US Shelf, using RLQ analysis.
